Am I required to buy it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

29.0% of Harris County's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 29.0% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood. Past aid paid here is in “Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 170,854 NFIP flood claims and $8.7 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2017, 2001 and 2016.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2017 ($5,368,875,040), 2001 ($869,126,798), 2016 ($444,449,489). Total paid $8,732,143,453: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 170,854 claims since 1978 against 231,234 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for 36.8% of insured single-family homes here: FEMA's records put their rebuilding cost above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 129,659 policies reporting one)36.8%Texas: 35.8%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)79.2%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 134,418 claims paid with a damage figure)5.3%

Rebuilding cost is the replacement-cost figure on single-family primary-home policies that report one; many owners insure to the building maximum even when that figure is lower, so the two shares measure different things. The damage share counts every paid claim with a damage figure, all building types.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

52.9% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $858, full-risk $1,064 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$858
  • Median full-risk premium$1,064
  • Pay below full-risk52.9% of 184,869Texas: 47.6%

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How much flood risk is here?

Very High for river flooding and Relatively High for coastal flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskRelatively High
  • Inland flood riskVery High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. A place with many valuable buildings can have a large total loss and a low loss per dollar, so the rating and the percentile below can differ. Coastal: FEMA models roughly $2.5 million of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 48% of U.S. counties. Inland: FEMA models roughly $1.1 billion of flood loss a year (buildings, people and farmland valued in dollars, insured or not; a model, not insurance payouts); per dollar of building value, that loss is higher than in about 86% of U.S. counties. Any loss figure is a whole-county model estimate, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data: NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 76,646 damage records from homes here that flooded more than once; 5,781 records are from homes on FEMA's severe repetitive loss list.

  • Repeat-flood damage records76,646
  • Records from homes on the severe repetitive loss list5,781

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid records since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved October 26, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $1.2 billion for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,364 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Hurricane aid includes wind damage. COVID, fire, ice-storm and tornado aid are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted. FEMA also publishes a separate official policy count, which we have not yet compared for Harris County.

In-force count: 231,234 policy units (from 222,995 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 222,995 of 222,995 fetched; claims: 170,854 of 170,854 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
